title: Starbursts in Virgo
caption: Starburst spiral galaxy NGC 4536, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 4536 · constellation Virgo · about 50 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This detailed Hubble portrait, taken with the Wide Field Camera 3, shows NGC 4536, a spiral galaxy roughly 50 million light-years away in Virgo, the Virgin. It is a starburst galaxy, a hub of extreme star formation.

How galaxies form and change over time is still far from fully understood, which is why starburst galaxies are so useful. In them, one region or many is forming stars at such a breakneck pace that the galaxy is consuming its gas faster than the supply can be topped up. Studying the conditions inside them tells astronomers a lot about how galaxies evolve.

Several things can set off such a frenzy, but every one of them needs a large enough supply of gas. A galaxy might gain it by passing very close to another galaxy, by colliding outright with one, or through some other event that squeezes a great deal of gas into a relatively small space, where it can collapse into new stars.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.45 x 2.72 arcminutes) and distance (50 million light years), the frame spans roughly 36,000 × 40,000 light-years. Its light set out about 50 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using visible and near-infrared filters. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the long exposure collects far more light than an eye could.
